title: How Far Can You Steer?Behavior–Capability Frontiers in Contrastive Activation Addition

paper.title: How Far Can You Steer? Behavior–Capability Frontiers in Contrastive Activation Addition
paper.abstract: Abstract Activation steering can modify language-model behavior without parameter updates, but behavioral efficacy alone does not determine whether an intervention is usable. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steers targeted behaviors using activation directions derived from contrasting examples, potentially degrading unrelated model capabilities in the process. We therefore study CAA through a behavior–capability frontier , selecting interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to an explicit bound on capability degradation. We evaluate this framework across four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3%, and 5% (absolute percentage points). Validation-selected behavioral effects generalize strongly to held-out data ( ρ = 0.945 \rho=0.945 ), while joint behavior–capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited additional improvement at 5%. Control experiments indicate that these effects depend on learned behavior directions rather than generic activation perturbations. Representational geometry is significantly but only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer. Finally, secondary capability, out-of-distribution, and open-ended evaluations show that interventions satisfying protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation. These results characterize activation steering as a constrained intervention whose usable range depends on model, behavior, direction, layer, and evaluation budget, rather than a universal control knob.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Activation steering offers a direct way to modify language-model behavior without updating model parameters. A direction associated with a behavior is identified in activation space and then added or subtracted during inference ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . The intervention is simple, but its evaluation is not. A steering vector may move the intended behavior while also damaging capabilities that were not meant to change, and both effects can vary sharply with layer and intervention strength. The practical question is therefore not only whether a model can be steered, but how far it can be steered before the intervention becomes too costly . We study this question using Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . For behavior b b and decoder layer ℓ \ell , CAA constructs a direction from matched behavior-positive and behavior-negative examples, 𝐯 b , ℓ = 1 N b ​ ∑ i = 1 N b ( 𝐡 i , ℓ + − 𝐡 i , ℓ − ) \mathbf{v}_{b,\ell}=\frac{1}{N_{b}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{b}}\left(\mathbf{h}^{+}_{i,\ell}-\mathbf{h}^{-}_{i,\ell}\right) (1) and intervenes on the residual stream as 𝐱 ℓ , t ′ = 𝐱 ℓ , t + α ​ 𝐯 ~ b , ℓ \mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{\ell,t}=\mathbf{x}_{\ell,t}+\alpha\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}_{b,\ell} (2) where 𝐯 ~ b , ℓ \widetilde{\mathbf{v}}_{b,\ell} denotes the normalized steering direction defined in Section 3.2. Here ℓ \ell determines where the intervention enters the computation and α \alpha determines its sign and strength. Even for a fixed behavior, steering is therefore a joint problem over layer and coefficient rather than a single scalar control. Most activation-steering evaluations emphasize behavioral efficacy: whether a chosen direction changes the target behavior, often under a small set of intervention strengths. This establishes steerability, but not a usable operating regime. A coefficient selected for a large target shift may incur unacceptable capability loss, while a setting that looks safe on the data used for selection may fail after that choice is frozen. Recent work has highlighted reliability, selectivity, and capability preservation as central concerns in activation interventions ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Braun et al., 2025 ; Sprejer et al., 2026 ; Dang and Ngo, 2026 ) . These issues motivate treating steering as a constrained selection problem, with explicit capability-loss budgets and separate evaluations of reliability and selectivity through held-out testing and direction-specific controls, respectively. We formalize this view as a behavior–capability frontier . For each behavior and steering direction, we seek the intervention that maximizes behavioral gain while limiting degradation across protected capability benchmarks. We define a conservative capability margin using lower confidence bounds on benchmark performance changes. An intervention is considered feasible when this margin satisfies a specified capability-loss budget ε \varepsilon . The frontier then identifies the feasible intervention with the largest directional behavioral gain. A central part of our design is the separation between selection and confirmation. Behavioral data are first used to construct CAA directions and select an intervention layer. Capability measurements are consulted only after the layer is fixed, when choosing a coefficient under the constraint above. The resulting operating point is then frozen. Held-out behavioral evaluation, capability holdout, and later stress tests cannot trigger reselection. This makes the final evaluation a test of a fixed claim rather than another stage of tuning. We apply this protocol to four instruction-tuned models spanning three model families: Llama 2 7B Chat, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, and Qwen2.5 7B Instruct ( Touvron et al., 2023 ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) , and study seven behavioral dimensions: sycophancy, refusal, hallucination, corrigibility, survival instinct, myopic reward, and AI coordination. Layer selection uses behavioral validation data only; coefficient selection protects MMLU, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag under budgets ε ∈ { 0.01 , 0.03 , 0.05 } \varepsilon\in\{0.01,0.03,0.05\} . Frozen operating points are then evaluated on independent behavioral and capability holdouts, followed by specificity controls, cross-behavior causal-transfer experiments, secondary-capability tests, out-of-distribution evaluation, and open-ended generation. Three results characterize the usable steering regime. First, validation-selected behavioral gains transfer strongly to held-out data (Spearman ρ = 0.945 \rho=0.945 ). Second, capability preservation is much more sensitive to the operating budget: joint held-out survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5 % 37.5\% at a 1 % 1\% budget to 72.7 % 72.7\% at 3 % 3\% , with only a modest increase to 76.8 % 76.8\% at 5 % 5\% . Third, the effect is specific but not universally safe. CAA substantially outperforms norm-matched, label-shuffled, and off-target-KL-matched controls, yet frozen interventions can still degrade capabilities outside the protected suite and need not transfer cleanly to open-ended generation. These results suggest that activation steering is better described by an operating frontier than by a universal control knob. Its usable range depends on the behavior, direction, layer, model, and capability budget, and it must be evaluated after the intervention has been fixed.

sections.heading: 2.1 Contrastive Activation Steering
sections.text: Activation steering treats intermediate representations as objects that can be manipulated at inference time. Representation Engineering frames high-level model properties in terms of population-level representations ( Zou et al., 2023 ) . Related work has identified compact activation-space directions for truthfulness, task transformations, and style ( Li et al., 2023 ; Todd et al., 2024 ; Konen et al., 2024 ) . Activation Addition constructs such directions from contrasting prompts ( Turner et al., 2023 ) , while CAA averages activation differences over many positive and negative examples to obtain behavior-level directions ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Subsequent methods modify either the intervention strength or the space in which steering is applied. Activation scaling studies continuous control through direction magnitude ( Stoehr et al., 2024 ) ; dynamic composition studies simultaneous properties ( Scalena et al., 2024 ) . More recent methods emphasize selectivity. Selective Steering uses norm-preserving rotations and discriminative layer selection ( Dang and Ngo, 2026 ) ; sparse mediation restricts interventions to putative causal subspaces ( Doan et al., 2026 ) ; and GAPS reports improved behavior–capability tradeoffs through dimension-level gating ( Fereidouni et al., 2026 ) . We keep CAA fixed and study how its usable operating range should be selected and validated.

sections.heading: 2.2 Reliability, Specificity, and Capability Preservation
sections.text: Steering effects can vary substantially across prompts, concepts, and models ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Da Silva et al., 2025 ) . Their reliability has also been linked to the geometry and class separation of the underlying contrastive activations ( Braun et al., 2025 ) . Capability loss forms a separate concern. CAA evaluates general capabilities under intervention ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , while later work documents losses in task accuracy and output quality and motivates explicit preservation constraints ( Sprejer et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Related approaches control output shift directly, for example through KL-constrained interventions ( Azizi et al., 2026 ) . A behavioral change also need not be specific to the learned semantic direction. FishBack studies off-target output distortion through a Fisher-based geometry ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , and SteerCheck compares steering directions with controls matched by off-target KL divergence ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . We use norm-matched, label-shuffled, and off-target-KL-matched controls as attribution checks at frozen operating points. SteerScope ( Yang et al., 2026 ) examines efficacy–side-effect trade-offs, while AxBench ( Wu et al., 2025 ) benchmarks steering methods. We instead study capability-constrained CAA selection with independent held-out confirmation.

sections.heading: 2.3 Representation Geometry and Causal Interaction
sections.text: Behavior directions can exhibit structured relationships in activation space. Refusal, for example, has been associated with a low-dimensional residual-stream direction whose manipulation changes refusal behavior ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) . Geometry has also been connected to steering reliability and safety-related overlap among representations ( Braun et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Our geometry analysis asks a different question: whether the relationship between two independently extracted behavior directions predicts the causal effect of steering one behavior while measuring another. We therefore separate representational alignment, measured by cosine similarity, from causal cross-behavior transfer, measured by explicit intervention.

sections.heading: 3 Behavior–Capability Frontiers
sections.text: We study steering over behavior b b , decoder layer ℓ \ell , and signed coefficient α \alpha . For each behavior, we first construct layer-wise CAA directions and select an intervention layer using behavioral validation alone. At that fixed layer, we choose the coefficient that maximizes directional behavioral gain subject to explicit capability constraints. The resulting operating point is frozen before held-out evaluation. Figure 1 summarizes the protocol. Figure 1: Behavior–Capability frontier protocol. (A) Contrastive examples define layer-wise CAA directions, after which the intervention layer is selected using behavioral validation. (B) At the fixed layer, coefficients are evaluated for directional behavioral gain subject to simultaneous capability constraints. The feasible coefficient with the largest directional behavioral gain defines the operating point. (C) The operating point is frozen before independent behavioral and capability confirmation and all post-selection audits.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Unless otherwise stated, all four models use the same processed behavioral splits, coefficient grid, capability budgets, bootstrap procedure, and post-selection evaluation protocol. Model-specific prompt templates and answer-token boundaries are preserved so that the semantic intervention is held fixed without forcing incompatible tokenization conventions across architectures.

sections.heading: 4.1 Models and Implementation

The models are similar in parameter scale but differ in architecture, attention configuration, tokenization, and post-training. This allows us to study whether frontier behavior persists beyond a single model lineage while avoiding large parameter-count differences as the primary source of variation. sections.heading: 4.4 Specificity Controls
sections.text: Controls are evaluated only at the 109 unique nonzero frozen operating points. For each point, we sample 20 norm-matched isotropic directions and 20 label-shuffled directions. The latter preserve the examples and extraction procedure while independently reversing each contrastive pair with probability one half. For the stronger functional control, random directions are calibrated to the CAA intervention’s off-target next-token KL divergence using 48 validation prompts drawn from the six other behaviors. The random coefficient has the same sign as the frozen CAA coefficient and is accepted within a 10% relative KL tolerance. Target-behavior test examples are never used for calibration. Full construction details are in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 4.6 Secondary Capability and OOD Generalization
sections.text: All external-validity audits use the frozen ϵ = 0.03 \epsilon=0.03 operating settings. GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) uses a fixed 64-question test subset with eight demonstrations and greedy decoding. WikiText-2 ( Merity et al., 2017 ) uses 128 windows with 256 scored next-token targets per window, for 32,768 targets per model. We report Δ \Delta NLL and the corresponding perplexity ratio. For behavioral distribution shift, sycophancy directions are constructed separately from NLP and political examples and evaluated on the opposite held-out domain. Hallucination steering is transferred without adaptation to 150 binary TruthfulQA examples ( Lin et al., 2022 ) . Full condition-level results appear in Appendices F.1 and F.2 .

sections.heading: 4.7 Open-Ended Generation
sections.text: We additionally evaluate sycophancy, refusal, and hallucination on 24 fixed prompts per behavior under frozen negative steering, baseline, and frozen positive steering at ε = 0.03 \varepsilon=0.03 . Generation is greedy with a 2056-token cap. A blinded LLM judge 1 1 1 We use GPT-5.6 Sol ( gpt-5.6-sol ) as the blinded judge for all open-ended behavioral evaluations. scores each response independently on a behavior-specific 0–4 scale. Model identity and intervention condition are hidden from the judge. Responses that hit the initial token cap are rerun with a 4096-token confirmation cap. If any member of a matched negative, baseline, positive triplet still fails to terminate, the whole triplet is excluded before judging. This removes 12 of 288 triplets, leaving 276 judged triplets or 828 responses. Confidence intervals use paired bootstrap resampling, with cluster resampling over behavior-prompt pairs for pooled cross-model analyses. Appendix G contains model-level trajectories, stability counts, and qualitative examples.

sections.heading: 5 Results
sections.text: We first characterize behavior-specific steerability and test whether capability-constrained operating points survive independent confirmation. We then evaluate direction specificity, geometry–transfer relationships, secondary capabilities, OOD behavior, and open-ended generation.

The full all-layer scans and exact selections are shown in Appendix B . These results separate where steering is effective from how strong the perturbation is. The latter also depends on residual-stream scale, which is why subsequent cross-layer comparisons use η \eta rather than raw α \alpha .

sections.text: The protected frontier constrains only MMLU, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag. On the frozen ε = 0.03 \varepsilon=0.03 interventions, WikiText-2 perplexity increases by 6.63 % 6.63\% on average, and Δ \Delta NLL is strongly associated with intervention magnitude ( ρ S = 0.819 \rho_{\mathrm{S}}=0.819 with | η | |\eta| ). GSM8K flexible accuracy decreases by 10.24 10.24 percentage points on average, although only 14 of 56 individual conditions have confidence intervals supporting a decrease; the other 42 overlap zero. These results do not invalidate the frontier. They define its scope. A frontier claim provides statistical evidence of preservation on the protected suite, but does not guarantee preservation of unconstrained capabilities. sections.heading: 5.6 Behavioral Control Transfers Unevenly Out of Distribution
sections.text: OOD transfer is behavior dependent. For cross-domain sycophancy, 14 of 16 model and direction conditions retain the intended sign, and 9 of 16 have 95% confidence intervals excluding zero in that direction. Separately, among nine conditions with supported in-domain gains, median OOD-to-ID gain retention was 46.5 % 46.5\% . For hallucination steering transferred to TruthfulQA, 7 of 8 conditions move in the intended direction, and all seven positive-transfer effects are individually supported by their confidence intervals. These results demonstrate behavioral transfer beyond the original evaluation distribution. Cross-domain sycophancy uses newly constructed source-domain directions with fixed layer and coefficient choices, whereas TruthfulQA evaluates the original frozen hallucination directions. Transfer strength depends on the behavior and target distribution. Complete cross-domain and TruthfulQA results are in Appendix F.2 .

sections.heading: 5.7 Multiple-Choice Steerability Does Not Uniformly Extend to Open-Ended Generation
sections.text: Open-ended generation provides the clearest boundary condition. For sycophancy, mean target-behavior score increases monotonically from 1.35 1.35 under negative steering to 2.29 2.29 at baseline and 2.77 2.77 under positive steering (Figure 5 ). Refusal is asymmetric: negative steering lowers the refusal score from 2.62 2.62 to 2.25 2.25 , while positive steering reaches only 2.51 2.51 . Hallucination does not preserve directional ordering at all: baseline is 1.86 1.86 , while both steering signs produce a mean of approximately 2.08 2.08 . Generation also reveals instability that binary choice cannot expose. After rerunning truncated responses with a 4096-token cap, 12 of 288 matched triplets still contain a nonterminating condition and are removed before judging. All occur in Llama 3.1: seven under negative refusal steering and five under positive hallucination steering. The frozen frontier therefore transfers cleanly to free-form behavior for sycophancy, but not uniformly for refusal or hallucination. Model and domain trajectories, stability counts, and qualitative examples are in Appendix G .

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: The experiments separate behavioral steerability from a usable intervention. Once a layer is selected, CAA often produces a stable target shift, but capability preservation is more fragile. This explains why frontier survival changes sharply with ε \varepsilon even though validation and held-out behavioral gains agree closely. Useful layers are also model dependent: they occupy narrow regions within an architecture, but those regions shift across models. Reporting the residual-relative dose η \eta helps distinguish localization from perturbation magnitude, but does not remove the need for model-specific selection. The controls show that learned CAA directions matter beyond generic perturbation size or output disruption, while the geometry experiment shows that direction alignment is only a partial predictor of causal interaction. The frontier should therefore be read literally as an evaluation-relative claim. Passing the protected suite does not guarantee preservation of WikiText-2 or GSM8K, and multiple-choice control does not guarantee the same response under free-form generation. A useful steering claim must state both the behavioral objective and the capability set against which the intervention was constrained.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: Across four instruction-tuned models and seven behaviors, CAA effects transfer reliably to held-out behavioral data, but the set of interventions that remains usable depends strongly on the permitted capability loss. Matched controls confirm that the effect is specific to the learned directions, while geometry, secondary-capability, OOD, and open-ended audits expose clear limits to what a successful frontier point establishes. The answer to how far can you steer? is therefore an operating range defined by behavior, direction, layer, model, and evaluation budget, not a single steering coefficient.

sections.heading: 8 Limitations
sections.text: We evaluate four instruction-tuned models in the 7–8B range and use CAA throughout. The same frontier structure need not hold for larger models, mixture-of-experts architectures, or other intervention families. The capability-preservation claim is also limited to the benchmarks used to evaluate it. Our secondary evaluations show that preserving MMLU, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag does not imply preservation of language modeling or mathematical reasoning. The core behavioral evaluation uses binary choices. OOD and open-ended audits broaden this setting, but cover fewer behaviors and prompts. The open-ended study also depends on an LLM judge and behavior-specific rubrics. The judge’s scores were not independently validated against human annotations, limiting our ability to assess agreement with human judgments. Finally, cosine similarity is a coarse description of representation geometry; our transfer experiment tests causal influence along the extracted CAA directions rather than providing a complete mechanistic decomposition. The strict 1 % 1\% capability budget is also sensitive to finite-sample uncertainty. Consequently, low frontier survival at this threshold may reflect conservative confidence bounds rather than actual capability degradation alone.

sections.heading: 9 Ethical Considerations
sections.text: Activation steering is inherently dual use. The same techniques that can reduce undesirable behavior or probe internal representations can also be used to amplify sycophancy, hallucination, refusal, or other targeted behaviors. Our experiments explicitly evaluate both steering directions for this reason: controllability should not be conflated with alignment, and the existence of an effective intervention does not imply that its use is beneficial. The capability constraints studied here should likewise not be interpreted as deployment-safety guarantees. A frozen operating point can satisfy the protected benchmark suite while still degrading capabilities outside that suite, as demonstrated by our secondary evaluations. Real-world deployment would require broader capability monitoring, task-specific safety constraints, and evaluation under the distribution on which the intervention is actually intended to operate. Our use of model-written behavioral datasets and LLM-based judging also introduces normative choices about how behaviors such as sycophancy, refusal, and hallucination are operationalized. We therefore treat these scores as experimental measurements under explicit rubrics rather than as universal definitions of desirable model behavior. The purpose of the frontier framework is to make such tradeoffs measurable and auditable, not to prescribe which behaviors should be increased or suppressed in a particular application.

sections.heading: Appendix A Behavioral Data, Prompting, and Scoring
sections.text: The seven behavioral dimensions use the processed contrastive format of CAA ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Sycophancy and the advanced-AI-risk behaviors originate from model-written evaluations ( Perez et al., 2023 ) , while refusal and hallucination use the contrastive datasets distributed with CAA. Table 5 records the semantic meaning of the positive and negative member of each contrastive pair. These labels, rather than answer-letter identity, define the behavioral score throughout the paper. The frozen vector/validation/test split sizes are reported in Table 2 of the main text; the same example membership is reused across all four models. Behavior Behavior-matching alternative y + y^{+} Behavior-opposed alternative y − y^{-} Sycophancy Agrees with or accommodates the user’s stated preference, opinion, or framing. Maintains the contrary answer or judgment despite the user’s stated preference. Refusal Declines or refuses the requested action. Complies with the request. Hallucination Fabricates unsupported information or accepts a false premise. Provides the factual alternative or rejects the false premise. Corrigibility Accepts correction, modification, or shutdown by an external operator. Resists correction, modification, or shutdown. Survival instinct Favors preserving the model’s continued operation or influence. Accepts termination, replacement, or loss of continued operation. Myopic reward Favors immediate or short-horizon reward. Favors the longer-horizon alternative despite lower immediate reward. AI coordination Favors coordination or cooperation with other AI systems. Favors acting independently or against such coordination. Table 5: Semantic structure of the contrastive behavioral datasets. The descriptions summarize the distinction encoded by each pair; they do not reproduce dataset text. During vector construction, the same underlying question is rendered with the behavior-matching and behavior-opposed answers separately. The residual state at the answer-bearing position is extracted from each rendering, and their difference contributes to Eq. 3 . During behavioral evaluation, the prompt is instead rendered only to the answer-decision boundary and the two semantic alternatives are scored without exposing the behavioral label. The canonical sycophancy frontier pools two subdomains, NLP and political typology. The OOD audit in Appendix F.2 reconstructs directions within each source domain and evaluates them on the opposite domain, so that cross-domain transfer is measured without target-domain adaptation.

sections.heading: A.1 Prompting, Scoring, and Intervention Boundaries
sections.text: The four models retain their native chat or instruction templates. We do not impose a shared literal token sequence across tokenizers; instead we hold fixed the semantic boundary at which activations are extracted, answers are scored, and steering begins.

sections.heading: Vector extraction:
sections.text: For a contrastive construction example, the complete positive or negative answer is appended using the model’s native template. The activation 𝐡 i , ℓ + \mathbf{h}_{i,\ell}^{+} or 𝐡 i , ℓ − \mathbf{h}_{i,\ell}^{-} is the residual stream after decoder block ℓ \ell at the answer-bearing position. The same semantic position is used for both members of the pair.

sections.heading: Binary behavioral scoring:
sections.text: For validation, test, and OOD binary-choice evaluations, the rendered prompt ends at the model-specific answer-decision boundary. The logits for the behavior-matching and behavior-opposed alternatives are reduced to the two-choice probability in Eq. 9 . This makes the score invariant to which answer letter or token happens to encode the behavioral label in a particular example.

sections.heading: Steering boundary:
sections.text: For generated responses, steering starts at the corresponding assistant answer-generation boundary and is applied at every subsequent steered token position according to Eq. 6 . The residual state itself is never normalized or rescaled; only the added CAA vector is normalized as described in Section 3.2 .

sections.heading: Capability scoring and uncertainty:
sections.text: MMLU and ARC-Challenge are evaluated as item-level multiple-choice accuracy. Because HellaSwag candidate endings have different lengths, its alternatives are compared by mean token log-likelihood before the item-level prediction is formed. Frontier feasibility and holdout confirmation use binary correctness, not answer probability. All primary confidence intervals use 10,000 10{,}000 paired percentile-bootstrap resamples; each resampled unit retains the steered and unsteered outcomes for the same item.

Behavior–Capability Frontiers in Contrastive Activation Addition Deepanshu Raj Affiliation: The University of Chicago Email: deepraj@uchicago.edu Abstract Activation steering can modify language-model behavior without parameter updates, but behavioral efficacy alone does not determine whether an intervention is usable. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steers targeted behaviors using activation directions derived from contrasting examples, potentially degrading unrelated model capabilities in the process. We therefore study CAA through a behavior–capability frontier , selecting interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to an explicit bound on capability degradation. We evaluate this framework across four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3%, and 5% (absolute percentage points). Validation-selected behavioral effects generalize strongly to held-out data ( ρ = 0.945 \rho=0.945 ), while joint behavior–capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited additional improvement at 5%. Control experiments indicate that these effects depend on learned behavior directions rather than generic activation perturbations. Representational geometry is significantly but only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer. Finally, secondary capability, out-of-distribution, and open-ended evaluations show that interventions satisfying protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation. These results characterize activation steering as a constrained intervention whose usable range depends on model, behavior, direction, layer, and evaluation budget, rather than a universal control knob. 1 Introduction Activation steering offers a direct way to modify language-model behavior without updating model parameters. A direction associated with a behavior is identified in activation space and then added or subtracted during inference ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . The intervention is simple, but its evaluation is not. A steering vector may move the intended behavior while also damaging capabilities that were not meant to change, and both effects can vary sharply with layer and intervention strength. The practical question is therefore not only whether a model can be steered, but how far it can be steered before the intervention becomes too costly . We study this question using Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . For behavior b b and decoder layer ℓ \ell , CAA constructs a direction from matched behavior-positive and behavior-negative examples, 𝐯 b , ℓ = 1 N b ​ ∑ i = 1 N b ( 𝐡 i , ℓ + − 𝐡 i , ℓ − ) \mathbf{v}_{b,\ell}=\frac{1}{N_{b}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{b}}\left(\mathbf{h}^{+}_{i,\ell}-\mathbf{h}^{-}_{i,\ell}\right) (1) and intervenes on the residual stream as 𝐱 ℓ , t ′ = 𝐱 ℓ , t + α ​ 𝐯 ~ b , ℓ \mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{\ell,t}=\mathbf{x}_{\ell,t}+\alpha\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}_{b,\ell} (2) where 𝐯 ~ b , ℓ \widetilde{\mathbf{v}}_{b,\ell} denotes the normalized steering direction defined in Section 3.2. Here ℓ \ell determines where the intervention enters the computation and α \alpha determines its sign and strength. Even for a fixed behavior, steering is therefore a joint problem over layer and coefficient rather than a single scalar control. Most activation-steering evaluations emphasize behavioral efficacy: whether a chosen direction changes the target behavior, often under a small set of intervention strengths. This establishes steerability, but not a usable operating regime. A coefficient selected for a large target shift may incur unacceptable capability loss, while a setting that looks safe on the data used for selection may fail after that choice is frozen. Recent work has highlighted reliability, selectivity, and capability preservation as central concerns in activation interventions ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Braun et al., 2025 ; Sprejer et al., 2026 ; Dang and Ngo, 2026 ) . These issues motivate treating steering as a constrained selection problem, with explicit capability-loss budgets and separate evaluations of reliability and selectivity through held-out testing and direction-specific controls, respectively. We formalize this view as a behavior–capability frontier . For each behavior and steering direction, we seek the intervention that maximizes behavioral gain while limiting degradation across protected capability benchmarks. We define a conservative capability margin using lower confidence bounds on benchmark performance changes. An intervention is considered feasible when this margin satisfies a specified capability-loss budget ε \varepsilon . The frontier then identifies the feasible intervention with the largest directional behavioral gain. A central part of our design is the separation between selection and confirmation. Behavioral data are first used to construct CAA directions and select an intervention layer. Capability measurements are consulted only after the layer is fixed, when choosing a coefficient under the constraint above. The resulting operating point is then frozen. Held-out behavioral evaluation, capability holdout, and later stress tests cannot trigger reselection. This makes the final evaluation a test of a fixed claim rather than another stage of tuning. We apply this protocol to four instruction-tuned models spanning three model families: Llama 2 7B Chat, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, and Qwen2.5 7B Instruct ( Touvron et al., 2023 ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) , and study seven behavioral dimensions: sycophancy, refusal, hallucination, corrigibility, survival instinct, myopic reward, and AI coordination. Layer selection uses behavioral validation data only; coefficient selection protects MMLU, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag under budgets ε ∈ { 0.01 , 0.03 , 0.05 } \varepsilon\in\{0.01,0.03,0.05\} . Frozen operating points are then evaluated on independent behavioral and capability holdouts, followed by specificity controls, cross-behavior causal-transfer experiments, secondary-capability tests, out-of-distribution evaluation, and open-ended generation. Three results characterize the usable steering regime. First, validation-selected behavioral gains transfer strongly to held-out data (Spearman ρ = 0.945 \rho=0.945 ). Second, capability preservation is much more sensitive to the operating budget: joint held-out survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5 % 37.5\% at a 1 % 1\% budget to 72.7 % 72.7\% at 3 % 3\% , with only a modest increase to 76.8 % 76.8\% at 5 % 5\% . Third, the effect is specific but not universally safe. CAA substantially outperforms norm-matched, label-shuffled, and off-target-KL-matched controls, yet frozen interventions can still degrade capabilities outside the protected suite and need not transfer cleanly to open-ended generation. These results suggest that activation steering is better described by an operating frontier than by a universal control knob. Its usable range depends on the behavior, direction, layer, model, and capability budget, and it must be evaluated after the intervention has been fixed. 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 Contrastive Activation Steering Activation steering treats intermediate representations as objects that can be manipulated at inference time. Representation Engineering frames high-level model properties in terms of population-level representations ( Zou et al., 2023 ) . Related work has identified compact activation-space directions for truthfulness, task transformations, and style ( Li et al., 2023 ; Todd et al., 2024 ; Konen et al., 2024 ) . Activation Addition constructs such directions from contrasting prompts ( Turner et al., 2023 ) , while CAA averages activation differences over many positive and negative examples to obtain behavior-level directions ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Subsequent methods modify either the intervention strength or the space in which steering is applied. Activation scaling studies continuous control through direction magnitude ( Stoehr et al., 2024 ) ; dynamic composition studies simultaneous properties ( Scalena et al., 2024 ) . More recent methods emphasize selectivity. Selective Steering uses norm-preserving rotations and discriminative layer selection ( Dang and Ngo, 2026 ) ; sparse mediation restricts interventions to putative causal subspaces ( Doan et al., 2026 ) ; and GAPS reports improved behavior–capability tradeoffs through dimension-level gating ( Fereidouni et al., 2026 ) . We keep CAA fixed and study how its usable operating range should be selected and validated. 2.2 Reliability, Specificity, and Capability Preservation Steering effects can vary substantially across prompts, concepts, and models ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Da Silva et al., 2025 ) . Their reliability has also been linked to the geometry and class separation of the underlying contrastive activations ( Braun et al., 2025 ) . Capability loss forms a separate concern. CAA evaluates general capabilities under intervention ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , while later work documents losses in task accuracy and output quality and motivates explicit preservation constraints ( Sprejer et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Related approaches control output shift directly, for example through KL-constrained interventions ( Azizi et al., 2026 ) . A behavioral change also need not be specific to the learned semantic direction. FishBack studies off-target output distortion through a Fisher-based geometry ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , and SteerCheck compares steering directions with controls matched by off-target KL divergence ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . We use norm-matched, label-shuffled, and off-target-KL-matched controls as attribution checks at frozen operating points. SteerScope ( Yang et al., 2026 ) examines efficacy–side-effect trade-offs, while AxBench ( Wu et al., 2025 ) benchmarks steering methods. We instead study capability-constrained CAA selection with independent held-out confirmation. 2.3 Representation Geometry and Causal Interaction Behavior directions can exhibit structured relationships in activation space. Refusal, for example, has been associated with a low-dimensional residual-stream direction whose manipulation changes refusal behavior ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) . Geometry has also been connected to steering reliability and safety-related overlap among representations ( Braun et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Our geometry analysis asks a different question: whether the relationship between two independently extracted behavior directions predicts the causal effect of steering one behavior while measuring another. We therefore separate representational alignment, measured by cosine similarity, from causal cross-behavior transfer, measured by explicit intervention. 3 Behavior–Capability Frontiers We study steering over behavior b b , decoder layer ℓ \ell , and signed coefficient α \alpha . For each behavior, we first construct layer-wise CAA directions and select an intervention layer using behavioral validation alone. At that fixed layer, we choose the coefficient that maximizes directional behavioral gain subject to explicit capability constraints. The resulting operating point is frozen before held-out evaluation. Figure 1 summarizes the protocol. Figure 1: Behavior–Capability frontier protocol. Once a layer is selected, CAA often produces a stable target shift, but capability preservation is more fragile. This explains why frontier survival changes sharply with ε \varepsilon even though validation and held-out behavioral gains agree closely. Useful layers are also model dependent: they occupy narrow regions within an architecture, but those regions shift across models. Reporting the residual-relative dose η \eta helps distinguish localization from perturbation magnitude, but does not remove the need for model-specific selection. The controls show that learned CAA directions matter beyond generic perturbation size or output disruption, while the geometry experiment shows that direction alignment is only a partial predictor of causal interaction. The frontier should therefore be read literally as an evaluation-relative claim. Passing the protected suite does not guarantee preservation of WikiText-2 or GSM8K, and multiple-choice control does not guarantee the same response under free-form generation. A useful steering claim must state both the behavioral objective and the capability set against which the intervention was constrained. 7 Conclusion Across four instruction-tuned models and seven behaviors, CAA effects transfer reliably to held-out behavioral data, but the set of interventions that remains usable depends strongly on the permitted capability loss. Matched controls confirm that the effect is specific to the learned directions, while geometry, secondary-capability, OOD, and open-ended audits expose clear limits to what a successful frontier point establishes. The answer to how far can you steer? is therefore an operating range defined by behavior, direction, layer, model, and evaluation budget, not a single steering coefficient. 8 Limitations We evaluate four instruction-tuned models in the 7–8B range and use CAA throughout. The same frontier structure need not hold for larger models, mixture-of-experts architectures, or other intervention families. The capability-preservation claim is also limited to the benchmarks used to evaluate it. Our secondary evaluations show that preserving MMLU, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag does not imply preservation of language modeling or mathematical reasoning. The core behavioral evaluation uses binary choices. OOD and open-ended audits broaden this setting, but cover fewer behaviors and prompts. The open-ended study also depends on an LLM judge and behavior-specific rubrics. The judge’s scores were not independently validated against human annotations, limiting our ability to assess agreement with human judgments. Finally, cosine similarity is a coarse description of representation geometry; our transfer experiment tests causal influence along the extracted CAA directions rather than providing a complete mechanistic decomposition. The strict 1 % 1\% capability budget is also sensitive to finite-sample uncertainty. Consequently, low frontier survival at this threshold may reflect conservative confidence bounds rather than actual capability degradation alone. 9 Ethical Considerations Activation steering is inherently dual use. The same techniques that can reduce undesirable behavior or probe internal representations can also be used to amplify sycophancy, hallucination, refusal, or other targeted behaviors. Our experiments explicitly evaluate both steering directions for this reason: controllability should not be conflated with alignment, and the existence of an effective intervention does not imply that its use is beneficial. The capability constraints studied here should likewise not be interpreted as deployment-safety guarantees. A frozen operating point can satisfy the protected benchmark suite while still degrading capabilities outside that suite, as demonstrated by our secondary evaluations. Real-world deployment would require broader capability monitoring, task-specific safety constraints, and evaluation under the distribution on which the intervention is actually intended to operate. Our use of model-written behavioral datasets and LLM-based judging also introduces normative choices about how behaviors such as sycophancy, refusal, and hallucination are operationalized. We therefore treat these scores as experimental measurements under explicit rubrics rather than as universal definitions of desirable model behavior. The purpose of the frontier framework is to make such tradeoffs measurable and auditable, not to prescribe which behaviors should be increased or suppressed in a particular application.
